questions.stem: A 6-year-old has periorbital edema and generalized swelling. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein. What is the main mechanism of the edema?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome: urinary protein loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure; renal edema is generalized and shows first in loose tissue such as the eyelids. A: Increased hydrostatic pressure follows impaired venous return (heart failure, venous obstruction). B: Lymphatic obstruction is inflammatory, neoplastic, post-surgical, or post-irradiation. D: Increased permeability is inflammatory. E: Arteriolar dilation (e.g., heat) raises hydrostatic pressure; not the cause here.

questions.stem: A pleural fluid sample has high protein content and many inflammatory cells. Which mechanism most likely produced it?

options.B: Increased hydrostatic pressure from heart failure

questions.explanation: Protein-rich inflammatory fluid is an exudate from increased permeability. A: Low oncotic pressure gives a transudate. B: Heart failure gives a transudate. C: Sodium retention gives a transudate. D: Cirrhosis gives a transudate.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing right heart failure has a liver with a mottled red and tan cut surface. Microscopy shows centrilobular necrosis and hemorrhage with preserved portal tracts. What is this?
questions.explanation: "Nutmeg liver": venous congestion damages the zone farthest from the blood supply (centrilobular). B: Steatosis is fat accumulation. C: Hepatitis cirrhosis has nodules and fibrous septa. D: Liver infarcts are rare (dual supply). E: Hemochromatosis is iron deposition.

questions.stem: An organ is engorged with blood and has a blue-red (cyanotic) color. Which mechanism and type of blood fit best?
questions.explanation: Congestion is passive: impaired venous outflow fills the organ with deoxygenated blood, giving a blue-red color. A: Active hyperemia (exercise, inflammation) makes tissue red with oxygenated blood. C: Stagnant venous blood is deoxygenated. D: Arteriolar dilation brings in oxygenated blood. E: Lymphatic blockage causes edema, not blood engorgement.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with chronic left heart failure has sputum containing macrophages with golden-brown cytoplasmic granules that stain with Prussian blue. What are these cells?
questions.explanation: Chronic pulmonary congestion ruptures capillaries; alveolar macrophages phagocytose RBCs and store iron as hemosiderin. A: Foam cells contain lipid. B: Anthracotic macrophages contain black carbon (Prussian blue negative). C: Langhans cells are granuloma giant cells. E: Reed–Sternberg cells are Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: Six months after mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation, a woman develops persistent swelling of the arm on the same side. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Post-surgical and post-irradiation lymphatic blockage causes lymphedema. A: Hydrostatic causes are impaired venous return (heart failure, venous obstruction) or arteriolar dilation. B: Low oncotic pressure follows hypoproteinemia (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition). C: Sodium retention is renal and causes generalized edema. D: Increased permeability is inflammatory.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with congestive heart failure has worsening leg edema. Besides raised venous pressure, which additional mechanism, triggered by reduced renal perfusion, worsens the edema?

options.B: Low oncotic pressure from urinary albumin loss

questions.explanation: Heart failure lowers renal perfusion, activating renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and increasing tubular sodium (and water) reabsorption. A: Lymphatic blockage is inflammatory, neoplastic, post-surgical, or post-irradiation. B: Urinary protein loss is nephrotic syndrome. D: Increased permeability is inflammatory. E: Arteriolar dilation is not the renal mechanism.
